subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: How does the reactivity of Group 2 metals change down the group, and why?
options: Increases, because ionisation energies decrease as outer electrons get further from the nucleus
questions.explain: Down Group 2 the outer electrons are lost more easily (lower ionisation energies) because they are further from the nucleus and more shielded, so reactivity increases.

questions.q: What are the products when calcium reacts with cold water?
questions.explain: Ca + 2H2O gives Ca(OH)2 + H2; Group 2 metals form the hydroxide and hydrogen gas with water.

questions.q: How many electrons can be held in total by a complete set of d orbitals in one sub-shell?
questions.explain: A d sub-shell contains five orbitals, each holding two electrons, giving a maximum of ten.

questions.q: What is the general trend in first ionisation energy across Period 3, and the main reason?
options: It stays constant because the shell is the same
It increases because nuclear charge increases while shielding stays similar
It decreases because atomic radius increases
questions.explain: First ionisation energy generally rises across Period 3 as increasing nuclear charge attracts the outer electrons more strongly with little change in shielding.

questions.q: After adding acidified silver nitrate, how can silver chloride be distinguished from silver iodide using ammonia?
options: AgCl is insoluble in all ammonia while AgI dissolves in dilute ammonia
Both dissolve readily in dilute ammonia
AgCl dissolves in dilute ammonia while AgI is insoluble even in concentrated ammonia
questions.explain: AgCl dissolves in dilute ammonia, AgBr dissolves only in concentrated ammonia, and AgI is insoluble in concentrated ammonia, allowing the halides to be distinguished.

questions.q: Which best explains the general decrease in atomic radius across Period 3 from Na to Ar?
options: Shielding increases faster than nuclear charge
Electrons are added to new shells, increasing the radius
The number of neutrons decreases across the period
Increasing nuclear charge pulls the same shell of electrons closer; shielding stays roughly constant
questions.explain: Across a period the nuclear charge rises while electrons enter the same shell with similar shielding, so the outer electrons are pulled in and the radius decreases.

questions.q: What is the maximum number of electrons that can occupy a single atomic orbital, and why?
options: Ten, the capacity of a d sub-shell
Two, because the Pauli exclusion principle requires opposite spins
Eight, to satisfy the octet rule
questions.explain: An orbital holds at most two electrons, which must have opposite spins according to the Pauli exclusion principle.

questions.q: What is the shape of an s orbital?
questions.explain: An s orbital is spherically symmetrical about the nucleus.

questions.q: When chlorine is added to cold dilute sodium hydroxide, what type of reaction occurs and what are the products?
options: Disproportionation, giving NaCl, NaClO and water
questions.explain: Cl2 + 2NaOH gives NaCl + NaClO + H2O; chlorine is simultaneously oxidised (to +1 in ClO-) and reduced (to -1 in Cl-), so it disproportionates.

questions.q: How does the solubility of the Group 2 hydroxides change down the group?
options: All Group 2 hydroxides are equally insoluble
Solubility is greatest for magnesium hydroxide
questions.explain: Group 2 hydroxide solubility increases down the group, so Mg(OH)2 is least soluble and Ba(OH)2 most soluble.

questions.q: Chlorine has two isotopes: 35Cl (75.0%) and 37Cl (25.0%). What is its relative atomic mass?
The mass spectrum of bromine (Br2) shows molecular ion peaks at m/z = 158, 160 and 162. This pattern arises because:
options: Bromine has three isotopes of equal abundance
Bromine has a relative atomic mass of 160
Br2 contains two atoms each of which can be 79Br or 81Br, giving combinations of 158, 160 and 162
questions.explain: With two roughly equally abundant isotopes (79Br and 81Br), Br2 gives 79+79=158, 79+81=160 and 81+81=162 in a 1:2:1 ratio.

questions.q: How many orbitals are present in a p sub-shell, and what shape are they?
questions.explain: A p sub-shell has three dumb-bell-shaped orbitals (px, py, pz) at right angles to each other.

questions.q: Why is the first ionisation energy of boron lower than that of beryllium, against the general trend across a period?
options: Boron has a half-filled 2p sub-shell that is destabilised
Boron's outer electron is in a 2p orbital of slightly higher energy than the 2s electron removed from beryllium
Boron has fewer protons than beryllium
questions.explain: The first electron removed from boron is a 2p electron, which is at a higher energy and less tightly held than beryllium's 2s electron.

questions.q: Across Period 3 from Na to Ar, first ionisation energy shows a general increase but with dips at Al and S. The dip at aluminium occurs because:
options: Aluminium experiences less shielding than magnesium
Aluminium has greater nuclear charge than sulfur
Aluminium's outer electron is a 3p electron, higher in energy than magnesium's 3s electron
questions.explain: Al's first electron is removed from a 3p orbital that lies above the filled 3s of magnesium, so less energy is needed.

questions.q: In the mass spectrum of a molecule, which peak corresponds to the molecular ion?
options: The peak with the highest m/z value (ignoring isotope peaks), equal to the relative molecular mass
The peak at the lowest m/z value
questions.explain: The molecular ion peak is the one at the highest m/z (the M peak), and its value equals the relative molecular mass.

questions.q: In which block of the periodic table is the element with configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p4?
questions.explain: The highest-energy electrons are in the 3p sub-shell, placing the element (sulfur) in the p-block.

questions.q: Why does sulfur (S8) have a higher melting point than phosphorus (P4) in Period 3?
options: S8 molecules are larger than P4 molecules, giving stronger van der Waals forces between them
Sulfur is a giant covalent structure
Sulfur has stronger covalent bonds within its molecules
questions.explain: Both are simple molecular solids, but the larger S8 molecule has more electrons and stronger London (van der Waals) forces than P4, so it melts at a higher temperature.

questions.q: Which sub-shell is filled immediately after the 3p sub-shell when building up electron configurations?
questions.explain: 4s is at a lower energy than 3d in the filling sequence, so 4s fills before 3d.

questions.q: What is observed when bromine water is added to potassium iodide solution?
options: The mixture darkens/turns brown as iodine is displaced
questions.explain: Bromine is a stronger oxidising agent than iodine, so it displaces iodine: Br2 + 2I- gives 2Br- + I2, producing a brown solution.

questions.q: Which statement about the 4s and 3d sub-shells is correct?
options: 4s fills first and 3d empties first on ionisation
4s fills first but 4s empties first on ionisation
questions.explain: 4s fills before 3d during the build-up, yet 4s electrons are removed before 3d electrons when the atom is ionised.

questions.q: What is the relative charge and relative mass of an electron (to the usual approximation)?
questions.explain: An electron has a relative charge of -1 and a relative mass of about 1/1836 of a proton.

questions.q: In the reaction Cl2 + H2O gives HCl + HClO, what are the oxidation states of chlorine in the products?
questions.explain: Chlorine is reduced to -1 in HCl and oxidised to +1 in HClO, a disproportionation of chlorine (0) used in water treatment.

questions.q: Calcium hydroxide is added to fields by farmers. What is its main agricultural use?
options: To neutralise acidic soils (raise the pH)
questions.explain: Ca(OH)2 is a base used to neutralise acidic soils, raising their pH.

questions.q: How does electronegativity change down Group 7, and why?
options: Stays the same throughout the group
Decreases, because the bonding electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded
questions.explain: Down Group 7 the atoms get larger and more shielded, so the nucleus attracts a bonding pair less strongly and electronegativity falls.

questions.q: During electron impact ionisation in a mass spectrometer, what happens to the sample particles?
options: A high-energy electron knocks out an electron, forming a 1+ positive ion
They are split into protons and neutrons
They are accelerated without any charge change
They gain an electron to form negative ions
questions.explain: A high-energy electron from an electron gun knocks an electron off each particle, typically forming 1+ ions.

questions.q: What is the main reason first ionisation energy generally decreases down a group?
options: Nuclear charge decreases down the group
The outer electron is in a higher shell, further from the nucleus and more shielded, despite increased nuclear charge
Electron-electron repulsion decreases down the group
questions.explain: Down a group the outer electron occupies a higher principal energy level and experiences more shielding, so it is held less strongly even though nuclear charge rises.

questions.q: In a time-of-flight mass spectrometer, two ions are accelerated to the same kinetic energy. Which reaches the detector first?
options: Both arrive at the same time
The ion with the larger mass
The ion with the greater charge always arrives first regardless of mass
The ion with the smaller mass
questions.explain: For equal kinetic energy, the lighter ion has a greater velocity and so a shorter time of flight.

questions.q: How does the solubility of the Group 2 sulfates change down the group?
options: Solubility decreases down the group, with BaSO4 essentially insoluble
questions.explain: Group 2 sulfate solubility decreases down the group; BaSO4 is essentially insoluble, which is why barium sulfate is used in the test for sulfate ions.

questions.q: What happens when chlorine water is added to potassium bromide solution?
options: A white precipitate of KCl forms
The solution turns orange as chlorine displaces bromine
questions.explain: Chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine, so it displaces bromine: Cl2 + 2Br- gives 2Cl- + Br2, giving an orange colour.
